rv.q: Bartlett Sher’s production, featuring legions of kids and lashings of costumes, purrs like a Rolls-Royce.
The King and I is undoubtedly dated, but it still retains its charm.
It’s a vibrant moment in Sher’s staid production, which takes the heavy-handed dialogue at a ponderous pace.
As drama, on the other hand, the saccharine piece lumbers along.
With the distance of time, this is a strange show.
When it’s presented as entertainingly as it is here, it’s hard to resist.
Golden Age musical pleasures with a dash of contemporary wisdom

Sher's direction more generally is also dull; the characters mostly present their lines and songs centre stage and facing front as if they cannot connect with the audience unless looking straight at them, undermining what they are saying and stretching both credulity and patience in a show that runs for just shy of three hours.
But as good as the songs are, you can’t get away from the fact this is a bit of a clunky, old-fashioned musical with themes that may have been acceptable in 1951 but are a little dated now.

cn.t: This lavish production delivers Rodgers and Hammerstein's gorgeous score and spectacle, but critics note the 1951 musical's colonialist storyline feels increasingly dated and problematic through a modern lens.
